nameStory: The hairy snail gets its common name from the tiny, fine hairs that cover its shell, giving it a distinctly fuzzy appearance. These microscopic bristles make it stand out from other smooth-shelled snails you might find crawling around your garden. The scientific name 'hispidus' actually means 'hairy' or 'bristly' in Latin, so both the common and scientific names tell the same fuzzy story!
description: The hairy snail is a small, terrestrial snail that breathes air rather than living in water. Its most distinctive feature is the covering of tiny, microscopic hairs that give its brownish shell a fuzzy, velvety appearance. These land snails are quite small, typically measuring less than half an inch across. They belong to a family known as the leaf snails, so named because many species in this group are often found among fallen leaves and plant debris.

idTips.label: Hairy shell surface
idTips.description: The shell feels slightly fuzzy or velvety to the touch due to microscopic bristles covering the surface - run your finger gently across it and you'll notice it's not smooth like most snails

idTips.label: Shell color and pattern
idTips.description: The shell is typically brownish with subtle darker bands or stripes that spiral around the whorls, giving it an earthy, mottled appearance

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: The shell is low and dome-shaped rather than tall and pointed, with a relatively wide opening and about 5-6 visible spiral whorls

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to easily sit on your thumbnail, usually less than half an inch across at its widest point

idTips.label: Terrestrial habitat
idTips.description: Found crawling on land among leaf litter and vegetation, never in ponds or streams like aquatic snails

habitat: Look for hairy snails in moist, shaded areas with rich soil and plenty of decaying organic matter. They favor gardens, wooded areas, and anywhere there's a good layer of fallen leaves or compost. These snails need humidity to survive, so you'll typically find them under logs, in leaf piles, or among dense vegetation where moisture is retained.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm and moisture increases from spring rains. Look for them emerging from winter hiding spots under logs and leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Active during humid weather, but may become less visible during hot, dry spells when they retreat to moister microhabitats.
seasonality.fall: Often more visible again as cooler, damper weather returns. They may be found feeding on decaying plant material.
seasonality.winter: Inactive and hidden deep in leaf litter, under logs, or in soil crevices where they can avoid freezing temperatures.

funFact: Despite being called 'hairy,' the snail's fuzzy shell covering actually helps it stay clean - the tiny bristles trap water droplets that wash dirt and debris off the shell, acting like a self-cleaning system that keeps the snail's home spotless!
confusionNotes: Most other small land snails in New England have smooth, shiny shells, making the hairy snail's fuzzy texture a dead giveaway. If you can't feel the fuzziness, you're probably looking at a different species entirely. Remember: fuzzy shell equals hairy snail!
contextualKnowledge: This species was previously classified under the scientific name Trichia hispida, so you might see it listed under that name in older field guides or references. The genus name was changed to Trochulus as scientists better understood the relationships between different snail groups.
compareHints: Since there are no other Trochulus species recorded in New England, compare the hairy snail to other small land snails in the leaf snail family. The hairy texture immediately sets it apart from smooth-shelled relatives. Other small terrestrial snails in the region will lack the distinctive fuzzy bristles that make this species unmistakable once you know what to feel for.
